preencoded.png
Why Automated LULC Classification Matters
1
Essential for 
Environmental Insight
LULC maps are fundamental 
tools for monitoring 
environmental changes, guiding 
urban expansion, informing 
climate models, and fostering 
sustainable development 
practices.
2
Efficiency Through 
Automation
Traditional manual 
classification processes are 
often time-consuming and prone 
to inconsistencies. Automation 
allows for rapid, repeatable, and 
highly scalable mapping, saving 
valuable resources.
3
Leveraging Cloud Power 
with GEE
Google Earth Engine (GEE) 
provides unparalleled cloud-
based access to vast satellite 
imagery datasets and powerful 
computing capabilities, enabling 
large-scale Land Use/Land 
Cover (LULC) analysis.

preencoded.png
Problem Formulation: Classifying 
Land Cover with Machine Learning
1
Supervised Classifiers
Widely adopted machine learning algorithms like Random Forest 
(RF), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Classification and 
Regression Trees (CART) are at the core of LULC classification.
2
Workflow for LULC Mapping
• Gather and prepare robust training data.
• Train the chosen classifier with the prepared data.
• Apply the trained model to classify satellite imagery.
• Validate results using accuracy metrics such as overall
     accuracy and kappa coefficient.
3
Proven Accuracy
For instance, applying RF and SVM to Sentinel-2 data has 
consistently achieved over 85% accuracy in distinguishing key 
classes like vegetation, built-up areas, barren land, and water 
bodies.

preencoded.png
Cutting-Edge Solutions for Enhanced LULC Mapping
Object-Oriented Classification
By segmenting images into meaningful clusters 
using algorithms like Simple Non-Iterative 
Clustering (SNIC) and extracting texture features 
(e.g., Gray-Level Co-occurrence Matrix - GLCM), 
object-oriented methods significantly improve 
accuracy in complex landscapes.
Deep Learning Integration
Vision Transformers (ViT) and other deep 
learning models, pre-trained on datasets such 
as EuroSAT, can be seamlessly deployed within 
GEE to generate highly detailed LULC maps with 
superior feature recognition capabilities.
Addressing Domain Shift
A key challenge is adapting models trained in one geographic 
region or with specific data types to perform effectively in 
new, distinct environments. Continuous model adaptation is 
crucial.

preencoded.png
Accuracy Assessment & Practical Applications
Quantifying Reliability
Confusion matrices and 
dedicated validation datasets 
are used to precisely quantify 
classification reliability, with 
typical overall accuracies 
ranging from 70% to 90%, 
depending on data quality and 
method complexity.
Supporting Critical Models
Automated LULC maps enhance 
climate models by providing 
more accurate meteorological 
parameters (e.g., temperature, 
wind speed), benefiting air 
pollution studies and optimizing 
renewable energy planning.
Real-World Success: Lake 
Trasimeno
A notable case study involved 
the Lake Trasimeno area in Italy, 
where object-oriented Random 
Forest classification on 
Sentinel-2 data achieved an 
impressive 89.3% accuracy, 
demonstrating real-world 
efficacy.

preencoded.png
Transforming Earth 
Observation with Automated 
LULC Mapping
The powerful synergy between Google Earth 
Engine's cloud infrastructure and advanced 
machine learning techniques is 
revolutionizing large-scale, precise LULC 
classification.
Continuous advancements in artificial 
intelligence and object-based analysis 
promise even finer resolution and faster 
insights into global land cover dynamics.
We must leverage these cutting-edge tools 
to enhance environmental decision-making, 
drive sustainable land management 
practices, and safeguard our planet 
worldwide.

Privacy Locker

Outline
Introduction to Project
Problem Formulation
Objectives of the work 
Methodology used
Results and Outputs
Conclusion
Future Scope
References
2

Introduction to Project
Privacy Locker is a full-stack web application for secure, private file storage and management.
Built with React.js (frontend), Node.js + Express.js (backend), and Cloudinary (secure file storage).
Features JWT-based authentication, AES-encrypted file storage and secure file upload/download/delete.
Files are encrypted using AES (CryptoJS) before being stored in Cloudinary.
Deployed on Render cloud platform with CI/CD automation via GitHub Actions.
Live at: https://privacy-locker.onrender.com/ | Source: github.com/sezal-jpg/Privacy-Locker
3

Background & Purpose
Growing digital privacy concerns: files stored on mainstream platforms lack user-controlled encryption.
Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive process user data under commercial policies without user-level encryption.
Privacy Locker places control in user hands: only authenticated, authorized users can access stored files.
Target users: individuals, professionals handling sensitive documents, and students/developers.
Course: Web Technologies / Full Stack Development | Chandigarh University, 2024-2025
4

Problem Formulation
Users lack a simple, self-deployable file storage solution that guarantees data privacy.
Existing platforms (Google Drive, Dropbox) do not provide transparent control over file access.
Commercial services may share or process user data for advertising under their terms of service.
Self-hosted solutions like Nextcloud require complex server infrastructure beyond typical student setup.
No lightweight, open-source, JWT-secured file locker exists for individual deployment with modern full-stack tech.
5

Objectives of the Work
Develop a responsive React.js frontend for seamless user experience (upload, download, delete files).
Implement a secure REST API backend using Node.js and Express.js.
Provide user authentication and session management using JSON Web Tokens (JWT).
Enable secure file upload, storage, and retrieval with Docker persistent volume management.
Deploy on Render cloud platform with automated CI/CD pipelines via GitHub Actions.
6

Methodology used
Three-Tier Architecture: React.js SPA (Nginx:3000) → Express API (Node.js:5000) → Cloudinary (cloud storage).
Authentication Flow: User registers → password hashed (bcrypt) → login returns signed JWT → token authorizes file endpoints.
File Flow: File → Base64 → AES Encryption → Uploaded to Cloudinary (raw storage)
Deployment: Render cloud platform
CI/CD: GitHub repo → GitHub Actions (build & test) → Render deploy hook → live production deployment.
7

Results & Outputs – Technology Stack
Frontend: React.js (SPA) | Backend: Node.js + Express.js (REST API) | Storage: Cloudinary.
Auth API: POST /api/auth/register (no auth) | POST /api/auth/login → returns JWT.
File API (JWT required): GET /api/files | POST /api/files/upload | Download handled via Cloudinary URL (encrypted file) | DELETE /api/files/:id.
User data stored temporarily (in-memory)Files stored in Cloudinary
Deployment: Render cloud platform
8

Results & Outputs – Testing
Deployment: Render cloud platform.
TC-01 to TC-03: User Registration and Login (valid/invalid credentials) – PASS.
TC-04 to TC-06: File Upload, Download, and Delete operations – PASS.
TC-07: Unauthenticated access returns HTTP 401 Unauthorized – PASS.
9

Results & Outputs – Performance & UI
API response time: 1-2 seconds under normal load on Render free tier.
Cold start on Render free tier: 20-30 seconds (container spin-down policy).
File uploads up to 10 MB tested successfully; Cloudinary queries return in under 100 ms.
Key screens: Login/Register page, Dashboard (file list with Download/Delete), File Upload with progress feedback.
Responsive UI accessible on desktop and mobile browsers; file ops completed in 2 clicks or fewer.
10

Conclusion
Privacy Locker successfully demonstrates a privacy-first, full-stack file storage system using modern web tech.
All stated objectives achieved: JWT auth, private file management, Docker deployment, and automated CI/CD.
Application is live and fully functional at https://privacy-locker.onrender.com/
Open source code available at github.com/sezal-jpg/Privacy-Locker.
Provided hands-on experience in full-stack development, security, and DevOps practices.
11

Future Scope
End-to-End Encryption: client-side file encryption before upload so server never accesses plaintext content.
File Sharing: time-limited, shareable download links for specific files.
Storage Quotas & File Preview: per-user limits with usage dashboards; in-browser preview for images, PDFs, and text files.
Two-Factor Authentication (2FA): TOTP-based 2FA for enhanced login security.
Mobile App & Kubernetes: React Native mobile client and Kubernetes migration for production-grade horizontal scaling.
12

References
[1] React Documentation – https://react.dev/learn (Accessed April 2025)
[2] Node.js Documentation – https://nodejs.org/en/docs (Accessed April 2025)
[3] Express.js Guide – https://expressjs.com/en/guide (Accessed April 2025)
[4] Cloudinary Documentation – https://www.cloudinary.com/docs/ (Accessed April 2025)
[5] JWT Introduction – https://jwt.io/introduction | [6] Docker Docs – https://docs.docker.com/
[6] GitHub Actions – https://docs.github.com/en/actions | [8] Render Docs – https://render.com/docs
[7] Privacy Locker GitHub – https://github.com/sezal-jpg/Privacy-Locker
[8] Privacy Locker Live Demo – https://privacy-locker.onrender.com/
13

Dating 102: Leave your ego at home. A lot of guys are too sensitive. If she giggles because you made a small mistake, instead of getting angry or defensive, try laughing at yourself. Remember she is as nervous as you are (or more!) and it could just be her nerves showing.

(that last one is something we should all aspire to all the time).
		





Dating 103: First date rules:
		Friends have set you up. What to do next?
		Call her or him and discuss the following: agree on where to go, what time, do you go together or meet there? What is the dress code? (that is kind of important to women). She does not want to dress to the nines and find you with old jeans and a faded T-shirt.
		This phone call is important for another reason. It breaks the ice and allows both to feel out the other person. Keep it short (less than 10 minutes).

Why Automated LULC Classification Matters
1
Essential for 
Environmental Insight
LULC maps are fundamental 
tools for monitoring 
environmental changes, guiding 
urban expansion, informing 
climate models, and fostering 
sustainable development 
practices.
2
Efficiency Through 
Automation
Traditional manual 
classification processes are 
often time-consuming and prone 
to inconsistencies. Automation 
allows for rapid, repeatable, and 
highly scalable mapping, saving

highly scalable mapping, saving 
valuable resources.
3
Leveraging Cloud Power 
with GEE
Google Earth Engine (GEE) 
provides unparalleled cloud-
based access to vast satellite 
imagery datasets and powerful 
computing capabilities, enabling 
large-scale Land Use/Land 
Cover (LULC) analysis.

preencoded.png
Problem Formulation: Classifying 
Land Cover with Machine Learning
1
Supervised Classifiers
Widely adopted machine learning algorithms like Random Forest 
(RF), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Classification and 
Regression Trees (CART) are at the core of LULC classification.
2
Workflow for LULC Mapping
• Gather and prepare robust training data.
• Train the chosen classifier with the prepared data.
• Apply the trained model to classify satellite imagery.

• Validate results using accuracy metrics such as overall
     accuracy and kappa coefficient.
3
Proven Accuracy
For instance, applying RF and SVM to Sentinel-2 data has 
consistently achieved over 85% accuracy in distinguishing key 
classes like vegetation, built-up areas, barren land, and water 
bodies.

preencoded.png
Cutting-Edge Solutions for Enhanced LULC Mapping
Object-Oriented Classification
By segmenting images into meaningful clusters 
using algorithms like Simple Non-Iterative 
Clustering (SNIC) and extracting texture features 
(e.g., Gray-Level Co-occurrence Matrix - GLCM), 
object-oriented methods significantly improve 
accuracy in complex landscapes.
Deep Learning Integration
Vision Transformers (ViT) and other deep 
learning models, pre-trained on datasets such

learning models, pre-trained on datasets such 
as EuroSAT, can be seamlessly deployed within 
GEE to generate highly detailed LULC maps with 
superior feature recognition capabilities.
Addressing Domain Shift
A key challenge is adapting models trained in one geographic 
region or with specific data types to perform effectively in 
new, distinct environments. Continuous model adaptation is 
crucial.

preencoded.png
Accuracy Assessment & Practical Applications
Quantifying Reliability
Confusion matrices and 
dedicated validation datasets 
are used to precisely quantify 
classification reliability, with 
typical overall accuracies 
ranging from 70% to 90%, 
depending on data quality and 
method complexity.
Supporting Critical Models
Automated LULC maps enhance 
climate models by providing 
more accurate meteorological 
parameters (e.g., temperature, 
wind speed), benefiting air

wind speed), benefiting air 
pollution studies and optimizing 
renewable energy planning.
Real-World Success: Lake 
Trasimeno
A notable case study involved 
the Lake Trasimeno area in Italy, 
where object-oriented Random 
Forest classification on 
Sentinel-2 data achieved an 
impressive 89.3% accuracy, 
demonstrating real-world 
efficacy.

preencoded.png

Observation with Automated 
LULC Mapping
The powerful synergy between Google Earth 
Engine's cloud infrastructure and advanced 
machine learning techniques is 
revolutionizing large-scale, precise LULC 
classification.
Continuous advancements in artificial 
intelligence and object-based analysis 
promise even finer resolution and faster 
insights into global land cover dynamics.

children.page_content:
​ Create an agent
This example demonstrates how to create a simple LangChain agent with a custom tool:
OpenAIGoogle GeminiClaude (Anthropic)OpenRouterFireworksBasetenOllamaAzureAWS BedrockHuggingFace# pip install -qU langchain "langchain[openai]"
from langchain.agents import create_agent

metadata.description: LangChain provides create_agent: a minimal, highly configurable agent harness. Compose exactly the agent your use case needs from model, tools, prompt, and middleware.
metadata.title: LangChain overview - Docs by LangChain

children.page_content:
def get_weather(city: str) -> str:
    """Get weather for a given city."""
    return f"It's always sunny in {city}!"

agent = create_agent(
    model="openai:gpt-5.5",
    tools=[get_weather],
    system_prompt="You are a helpful assistant",
)

    model="google_genai:gemini-2.5-flash-lite",

children.page_content:
​ Create an agent
This example demonstrates how to create a simple LangChain agent with a custom tool:
OpenAIGoogle GeminiClaude (Anthropic)OpenRouterFireworksBasetenOllamaAzureAWS BedrockHuggingFace# pip install -qU langchain "langchain[openai]"
from langchain.agents import create_agent

metadata.description: LangChain provides create_agent: a minimal, highly configurable agent harness. Compose exactly the agent your use case needs from model, tools, prompt, and middleware.
metadata.title: LangChain overview - Docs by LangChain

children.page_content:
def get_weather(city: str) -> str:
    """Get weather for a given city."""
    return f"It's always sunny in {city}!"

agent = create_agent(
    model="openai:gpt-5.5",
    tools=[get_weather],
    system_prompt="You are a helpful assistant",
)

        What is a context window?

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content:
What is a context window?



The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at any one time. A larger context window enables an AI model to process longer inputs and incorporate a greater amount of information into each output.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: An LLM’s context window can be thought of as the equivalent of its working memory. It determines how long of a conversation it can carry out without forgetting details from earlier in the exchange. It also determines the maximum size of documents or code samples that it can process at once. When a prompt, conversation, document or code base exceeds an artificial intelligence model’s context window, it must be truncated or summarized for the model to proceed.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: Generally speaking, increasing an LLM’s context window size translates to increased accuracy, fewer hallucinations, more coherent model responses, longer conversations and an improved ability to analyze longer sequences of data. However, increasing context length is not without tradeoffs: it often entails increased computational power requirements—and therefore increased costs—and a potential increase in vulnerability to adversarial attacks.

        Context windows and tokenization

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: In real-world terms, the context length of a language model is measured not in words, but in tokens. To understand how context windows work in practice, it’s important to understand how these tokens work.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: The way LLMs process language is fundamentally different from the way humans do. Whereas the smallest unit of information we use to represent language is a single character—such as a letter, number or punctuation mark—the smallest unit of language that AI models use is a token. To train a model to understand language, each token is assigned an ID number; these ID numbers, rather than the words or even the tokens themselves, are used to train the model. This tokenization of language

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: to train the model. This tokenization of language significantly reduces the computational power needed to process and learn from the text.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content:
There is a wide variance in the amount of text that one token can represent: a token can stand in for a single character, a part of a word (such as a suffix or prefix), a whole word or even a short multiword phrase. Consider the different roles played by the letter “a ” in the following examples:
“Jeff drove a car.”

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content:
Here, “a“ is an entire word. In this situation, it would be represented by a distinct token.
“Jeff is amoral.”

Here,  “a“ is not a word, but its addition to moral significantly changes the meaning of the word. Amoral would therefore be represented by two distinct tokens: a token for a and another for moral.
"Jeff loves his cat."

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: Here, a is simply a letter in the word “cat.” It carries no semantic meaning unto itself and would, therefore, not need to be represented by a distinct token.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: There is no fixed word-to-token “exchange rate,” and different models or tokenizers—a modular subset of a larger model responsible for tokenization—might tokenize the same passage of writing differently. Efficient tokenization can help increase the actual amount of text that fits within the confines of a context window. But for general purposes, a decent estimate would be roughly 1.5 tokens per word. The Tokenizer Playgroundon Hugging Face is an easy way to see and experiment with how different

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: easy way to see and experiment with how different models tokenize text inputs.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: Variations in linguistic structure and representation in training data can result in some languages being more efficiently tokenized than others. For example, an October 2024 study explored an example of the same sentence being tokenized in both English and Telugu. Despite the Telugu translation having significantly fewer characters than its English equivalent, it resulted in over 7 times the number of tokens in context.

children.page_content: Why do models have a maximum context length?

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: Though context windows are usually associated with LLMs used for summarization, generating text and other natural language processing (NLP) tasks, context length as a technical consideration is not exclusive to language models. The notion of a context window is relevant to any machine learning model that uses the transformer architecture, which comprises most modern generative AI models, including nearly all LLMs.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: Transformer models use a self-attention mechanism to calculate the relationships and dependencies between different parts of an input (like words at the beginning and end of a paragraph). Mathematically speaking, a self-attention mechanism computes vectors of weights for each token in a sequence of text, in which each weight represents how relevant that token is to others in the sequence. An autoregressive LLM iteratively consults those weights each time it generates the next word of its

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: each time it generates the next word of its output. The size of the context window determines the maximum number of tokens that the model can “pay attention to” at any one time.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: It's worth noting that the text of the actual user input is often not the only thing taking up space within a model’s context window. In many cases, such as with chatbots, models are also provided with a “system prompt”—often hidden from the user—that conditions their behavior and governs other aspects of the conversation. Supplementary information drawn from external data sources for retrieval augmented generation (RAG) is likewise stored within the context window during inference. Special

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: the context window during inference. Special characters, line breaks and other formatting measures also consume some portion of the available context.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: It’s also worth noting that language models are not the only neural networks that utilize transformers. For instance, some diffusion models used for image generation incorporate self-attention into their architecture. In their case, the context being attended to is not between tokens representing words (or parts of words) in written content, but between pixels in an image. In such a model, context length would apply to the number of pixels whose relationships the model must understand. Its

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: relationships the model must understand. Its context window could be exceeded by a high-resolution image containing too many pixels to process at once.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: Context windows and computing resources

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: Equipping a model with a large context window comes at a cost, both figuratively and literally. Compute requirements scale quadratically with the length of a sequence: for instance, if the number of input tokens doubles, the model needs 4 times as much processing power to handle it.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: Similarly, increasing context length can also slow down outputs. Each time the model autoregressively predicts the next token in a sequence, it computes the relationships between that token and every single preceding token in the sequence. Inference might be relatively fast at the beginning of a sequence or conversation but progressively become slower as the context length increases. This is problematic for use cases requiring near-instantaneous inference in real-time.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: Recent advancements in average context length for language models have been partially enabled by new techniques to increase inference speed and efficiency enough to sufficiently offset these inherent tradeoffs. These optimization techniques have allowed even small, open source modern LLMs to offer context windows exponentially larger than that of the original GPT-3.5 model that launched OpenAI’s ChatGPT in late 2022.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content:
Challenges of long context windows



Even when adequate measures are taken to offset the tradeoffs in computation requirements and processing speed, extending a model’s context length limit introduces additional challenges and complications.




Performance challenges

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: Like people, LLMs can be overwhelmed by an abundance of extra detail. They can also get lazy and take cognitive shortcuts. A 2023 paper found that LLMs don’t “robustly make use of information in long input contexts.” More specifically, the authors observed that models perform best when relevant information is toward the beginning or end of the input context. They further observed that performance degrades when the model must carefully consider the information in the middle of long contexts.1

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: Novel methods to improve the efficacy of the transformer’s self-attention mechanism itself, such as rotary position embedding (RoPE), aim to modify the positional encoding of tokens in attention vectors. The widespread adoption of RoPE-based methods has yielded enhanced performance and speed on tasks involving tokens at a large distance from one another.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: Ongoing research has produced a number of benchmarks designed to measure an LLM’s ability to effectively find and use relevant information with large passages, such as needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH),  RULER and LongBench.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content:
Safety and cybersecurity challenges


A longer context window might also have the unintended effect of presenting a longer attack surface for adversarial prompts. Recent research from Anthropic demonstrated that increasing a model’s context length also increases its vulnerability to “jailbreaking” and (subsequently) being provoked to produce harmful responses.2






        Context window sizes of prominent LLMs

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: The average context window of a large language model has grown exponentially since the original generative pretrained transformers (GPTs) were released. To date, each successive generation of LLMs has typically entailed significantly longer context lengths. At present, the largest context window offered by a prominent commercial model is over 1 million tokens. It remains to be seen whether context windows will continue to expand or if we’re already approaching the upper limit of practical

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: already approaching the upper limit of practical necessity.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: For reference, here are the current context lengths offered by some commonly cited models and model families as of October 2024.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content:
OpenAI's GPT series


The GPT-3.5 model that powered the launch of ChatGPT had a maximum context length of 4,096 tokens, later expanded to 8,192 tokens with GPT-3.5-Turbo.

At launch, GPT-4 had that same 8,192-token context length. Though the context window of both GPT-4 and GPT-4-Turbo has since been increased to 128,000 tokens, its max output tokens remain capped at 4,096 tokens.

Meta Llama models


The original Llama models had a maximum context length of 2,048 tokens, which was doubled to 4,096 tokens for Llama 2. During their launch in April 2024, Llama 3 models offered a context window of roughly 8,000 tokens.
Llama’s context length was significantly increased with the launch of Llama 3.1 models, which offered 128,000-token long context windows. Llama 3.2 models likewise have a maximum context length of 128,000 tokens.

Mistral Large 2, the flagship model offered by Mistral AI, has a context window of 128,000 tokens.




Google Gemini models


Google’s Gemini series of models offers what is currently the largest context window amongst commercial language models.         What is a context window?

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content:
What is a context window?



The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at any one time. A larger context window enables an AI model to process longer inputs and incorporate a greater amount of information into each output.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: An LLM’s context window can be thought of as the equivalent of its working memory. It determines how long of a conversation it can carry out without forgetting details from earlier in the exchange. It also determines the maximum size of documents or code samples that it can process at once. When a prompt, conversation, document or code base exceeds an artificial intelligence model’s context window, it must be truncated or summarized for the model to proceed.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: Generally speaking, increasing an LLM’s context window size translates to increased accuracy, fewer hallucinations, more coherent model responses, longer conversations and an improved ability to analyze longer sequences of data. However, increasing context length is not without tradeoffs: it often entails increased computational power requirements—and therefore increased costs—and a potential increase in vulnerability to adversarial attacks.

metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

        Context windows and tokenization

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: In real-world terms, the context length of a language model is measured not in words, but in tokens. To understand how context windows work in practice, it’s important to understand how these tokens work.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: The way LLMs process language is fundamentally different from the way humans do. Whereas the smallest unit of information we use to represent language is a single character—such as a letter, number or punctuation mark—the smallest unit of language that AI models use is a token. To train a model to understand language, each token is assigned an ID number; these ID numbers, rather than the words or even the tokens themselves, are used to train the model. This tokenization of language

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: to train the model. This tokenization of language significantly reduces the computational power needed to process and learn from the text.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content:
There is a wide variance in the amount of text that one token can represent: a token can stand in for a single character, a part of a word (such as a suffix or prefix), a whole word or even a short multiword phrase. Consider the different roles played by the letter “a ” in the following examples:
“Jeff drove a car.”

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content:
Here, “a“ is an entire word. In this situation, it would be represented by a distinct token.
“Jeff is amoral.”

Here,  “a“ is not a word, but its addition to moral significantly changes the meaning of the word. Amoral would therefore be represented by two distinct tokens: a token for a and another for moral.
"Jeff loves his cat."

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: Here, a is simply a letter in the word “cat.” It carries no semantic meaning unto itself and would, therefore, not need to be represented by a distinct token.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: There is no fixed word-to-token “exchange rate,” and different models or tokenizers—a modular subset of a larger model responsible for tokenization—might tokenize the same passage of writing differently. Efficient tokenization can help increase the actual amount of text that fits within the confines of a context window. But for general purposes, a decent estimate would be roughly 1.5 tokens per word. The Tokenizer Playgroundon Hugging Face is an easy way to see and experiment with how different

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: easy way to see and experiment with how different models tokenize text inputs.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: Variations in linguistic structure and representation in training data can result in some languages being more efficiently tokenized than others. For example, an October 2024 study explored an example of the same sentence being tokenized in both English and Telugu. Despite the Telugu translation having significantly fewer characters than its English equivalent, it resulted in over 7 times the number of tokens in context.

children.page_content: Why do models have a maximum context length?

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: Though context windows are usually associated with LLMs used for summarization, generating text and other natural language processing (NLP) tasks, context length as a technical consideration is not exclusive to language models. The notion of a context window is relevant to any machine learning model that uses the transformer architecture, which comprises most modern generative AI models, including nearly all LLMs.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: Transformer models use a self-attention mechanism to calculate the relationships and dependencies between different parts of an input (like words at the beginning and end of a paragraph). Mathematically speaking, a self-attention mechanism computes vectors of weights for each token in a sequence of text, in which each weight represents how relevant that token is to others in the sequence. An autoregressive LLM iteratively consults those weights each time it generates the next word of its

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: each time it generates the next word of its output. The size of the context window determines the maximum number of tokens that the model can “pay attention to” at any one time.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: It's worth noting that the text of the actual user input is often not the only thing taking up space within a model’s context window. In many cases, such as with chatbots, models are also provided with a “system prompt”—often hidden from the user—that conditions their behavior and governs other aspects of the conversation. Supplementary information drawn from external data sources for retrieval augmented generation (RAG) is likewise stored within the context window during inference. Special

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: the context window during inference. Special characters, line breaks and other formatting measures also consume some portion of the available context.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: It’s also worth noting that language models are not the only neural networks that utilize transformers. For instance, some diffusion models used for image generation incorporate self-attention into their architecture. In their case, the context being attended to is not between tokens representing words (or parts of words) in written content, but between pixels in an image. In such a model, context length would apply to the number of pixels whose relationships the model must understand. Its

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: relationships the model must understand. Its context window could be exceeded by a high-resolution image containing too many pixels to process at once.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: Context windows and computing resources

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: Equipping a model with a large context window comes at a cost, both figuratively and literally. Compute requirements scale quadratically with the length of a sequence: for instance, if the number of input tokens doubles, the model needs 4 times as much processing power to handle it.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: Similarly, increasing context length can also slow down outputs. Each time the model autoregressively predicts the next token in a sequence, it computes the relationships between that token and every single preceding token in the sequence. Inference might be relatively fast at the beginning of a sequence or conversation but progressively become slower as the context length increases. This is problematic for use cases requiring near-instantaneous inference in real-time.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: Recent advancements in average context length for language models have been partially enabled by new techniques to increase inference speed and efficiency enough to sufficiently offset these inherent tradeoffs. These optimization techniques have allowed even small, open source modern LLMs to offer context windows exponentially larger than that of the original GPT-3.5 model that launched OpenAI’s ChatGPT in late 2022.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content:
Challenges of long context windows



Even when adequate measures are taken to offset the tradeoffs in computation requirements and processing speed, extending a model’s context length limit introduces additional challenges and complications.




Performance challenges

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: Like people, LLMs can be overwhelmed by an abundance of extra detail. They can also get lazy and take cognitive shortcuts. A 2023 paper found that LLMs don’t “robustly make use of information in long input contexts.” More specifically, the authors observed that models perform best when relevant information is toward the beginning or end of the input context. They further observed that performance degrades when the model must carefully consider the information in the middle of long contexts.1

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: Novel methods to improve the efficacy of the transformer’s self-attention mechanism itself, such as rotary position embedding (RoPE), aim to modify the positional encoding of tokens in attention vectors. The widespread adoption of RoPE-based methods has yielded enhanced performance and speed on tasks involving tokens at a large distance from one another.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: Ongoing research has produced a number of benchmarks designed to measure an LLM’s ability to effectively find and use relevant information with large passages, such as needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH),  RULER and LongBench.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content:
Safety and cybersecurity challenges


A longer context window might also have the unintended effect of presenting a longer attack surface for adversarial prompts. Recent research from Anthropic demonstrated that increasing a model’s context length also increases its vulnerability to “jailbreaking” and (subsequently) being provoked to produce harmful responses.2






        Context window sizes of prominent LLMs

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: The average context window of a large language model has grown exponentially since the original generative pretrained transformers (GPTs) were released. To date, each successive generation of LLMs has typically entailed significantly longer context lengths. At present, the largest context window offered by a prominent commercial model is over 1 million tokens. It remains to be seen whether context windows will continue to expand or if we’re already approaching the upper limit of practical

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: already approaching the upper limit of practical necessity.

metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content: For reference, here are the current context lengths offered by some commonly cited models and model families as of October 2024.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content:
OpenAI's GPT series


The GPT-3.5 model that powered the launch of ChatGPT had a maximum context length of 4,096 tokens, later expanded to 8,192 tokens with GPT-3.5-Turbo.

At launch, GPT-4 had that same 8,192-token context length. Though the context window of both GPT-4 and GPT-4-Turbo has since been increased to 128,000 tokens, its max output tokens remain capped at 4,096 tokens.

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content:
Both GPT-4o and GPT-4o mini have a context window of 128,000 tokens, with output capped at 16,384 tokens.
The new o1 model family likewise offers a context window of 128,000 tokens, though they offer greater output context length.




Meta Llama models

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content:
Meta Llama models


The original Llama models had a maximum context length of 2,048 tokens, which was doubled to 4,096 tokens for Llama 2. During their launch in April 2024, Llama 3 models offered a context window of roughly 8,000 tokens.
Llama’s context length was significantly increased with the launch of Llama 3.1 models, which offered 128,000-token long context windows. Llama 3.2 models likewise have a maximum context length of 128,000 tokens.




Mistral Large 2

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content:
Mistral Large 2


Mistral Large 2, the flagship model offered by Mistral AI, has a context window of 128,000 tokens.




Google Gemini models


Google’s Gemini series of models offers what is currently the largest context window amongst commercial language models. Gemini 1.5 Pro, Google’s flagship model, offers a context length of up to 2 million tokens. Other Gemini 1.5 models, such as Gemini 1.5 Flash, have a context window of 1 million tokens.




Anthropic's Claude models

metadata.description: The context window (or “context length”) of a large language model (LLM) is the amount of text, in tokens, that the model can consider or “remember” at once.
metadata.title: What is a context window? | IBM

children.page_content:
Anthropic's Claude models


Anthropic’s latest Claude models, such as the Claude 3.5 Sonnet, offer a standard context window of about 200,000 tokens. In early September 2024, Anthropic announced that the models accessed through its new “Claude Enterprise” plan would offer an expanded 500,000 token context window.

Machine learning, and in particular deep learning, is the backbone of most modern AI systems.

        What is machine learning?

metadata.description: Machine learning is the subset of AI focused on algorithms that analyze and “learn” the patterns of training data in order to make accurate inferences about new data.
metadata.title: What is Machine Learning? | IBM

children.page_content:
What is machine learning?
    


Machine learning is the subset of artificial intelligence (AI) focused on algorithms that can “learn” the patterns of training data and, subsequently, make accurate inferences about new data. This pattern recognition ability enables machine learning models to make decisions or predictions without explicit, hard-coded instructions.

metadata.description: Machine learning is the subset of AI focused on algorithms that analyze and “learn” the patterns of training data in order to make accurate inferences about new data.
metadata.title: What is Machine Learning? | IBM

children.page_content: Machine learning has come to dominate the field of AI: it provides the backbone of most modern AI systems, from forecasting models to autonomous vehicles to large language models (LLMs) and other generative AI tools.

metadata.description: Machine learning is the subset of AI focused on algorithms that analyze and “learn” the patterns of training data in order to make accurate inferences about new data.
metadata.title: What is Machine Learning? | IBM

children.page_content: The central premise of machine learning (ML) is that if you optimize a model’s performance on a dataset of tasks that adequately resemble the real-world problems it will be used for—through a process called model training—the model can make accurate predictions on the new data it sees in its ultimate use case.

metadata.description: Machine learning is the subset of AI focused on algorithms that analyze and “learn” the patterns of training data in order to make accurate inferences about new data.
metadata.title: What is Machine Learning? | IBM

children.page_content: Training itself is simply a means to an end: generalization, the translation of strong performance on training data to useful results in real-world scenarios, is the fundamental goal of machine learning. In essence, a trained model is applying patterns it learned from training data to infer the correct output for a real-world task: the deployment of an AI model is therefore called AI inference.

metadata.description: Machine learning is the subset of AI focused on algorithms that analyze and “learn” the patterns of training data in order to make accurate inferences about new data.
metadata.title: What is Machine Learning? | IBM

children.page_content: Deep learning, the subset of machine learning driven by large—or rather, “deep”—artificial neural networks, has emerged over the past few decades as the state-of-the-art AI model architecture across nearly every domain in which AI is used. In contrast to the explicitly defined algorithms of traditional machine learning, deep learning relies on distributed “networks” of mathematical operations that provide an unparalleled ability to learn the intricate nuances of very complex data. Because deep

metadata.description: Machine learning is the subset of AI focused on algorithms that analyze and “learn” the patterns of training data in order to make accurate inferences about new data.
metadata.title: What is Machine Learning? | IBM

children.page_content: nuances of very complex data. Because deep learning requires very large amounts of data and computational resources, its advent has coincided with the escalated importance “big data” and graphics processing units (GPUs).

metadata.description: Machine learning is the subset of AI focused on algorithms that analyze and “learn” the patterns of training data in order to make accurate inferences about new data.
metadata.title: What is Machine Learning? | IBM

children.page_content: The discipline of machine learning is closely intertwined with that of data science. In a sense, machine learning can be understood as a collection of algorithms and techniques to automate data analysis and (more importantly) apply learnings from that analysis to the autonomous execution of relevant tasks.

metadata.description: Machine learning is the subset of AI focused on algorithms that analyze and “learn” the patterns of training data in order to make accurate inferences about new data.
metadata.title: What is Machine Learning? | IBM

children.page_content: The origin of the term (albeit not the core concept itself) is often attributed to Arthur L. Samuel’s 1959 article in IBM Journal, “Some Studies in Machine Learning Using the Game of Checkers.” In the paper’s introduction, Samuel neatly articulates machine learning’s ideal outcome: “a computer can be programmed so that it will learn to play a better game of checkers than can be played by the person who wrote the program.”1

metadata.description: Machine learning is the subset of AI focused on algorithms that analyze and “learn” the patterns of training data in order to make accurate inferences about new data.
metadata.title: What is Machine Learning? | IBM

children.page_content: Machine learning vs. artificial intelligence

metadata.description: Machine learning is the subset of AI focused on algorithms that analyze and “learn” the patterns of training data in order to make accurate inferences about new data.
metadata.title: What is Machine Learning? | IBM

children.page_content: Though “machine learning” and “artificial intelligence” are often used interchangeably, they are not quite synonymous. In short: all machine learning is AI, but not all AI is machine learning.

metadata.description: Machine learning is the subset of AI focused on algorithms that analyze and “learn” the patterns of training data in order to make accurate inferences about new data.
metadata.title: What is Machine Learning? | IBM

children.page_content: In the popular imagination, “AI” is usually associated with science fiction—typically through depictions of what’s more properly called artificial general intelligence (AGI), like HAL 9000 in 2001: A Space Odyssey or Ava in Ex Machina—or, more recently, with generative AI. But “artificial intelligence” is a catch-all term for any program that can use information to make decisions or predictions without active human involvement.

metadata.description: Machine learning is the subset of AI focused on algorithms that analyze and “learn” the patterns of training data in order to make accurate inferences about new data.
metadata.title: What is Machine Learning? | IBM

children.page_content:
The most elementary AI systems are a series of if-then-else statements, with rules and logic programmed explicitly by a data scientist.  At the simplest level, even a rudimentary thermostat is a rules-based AI system: when programmed with simple rules like 
IF room_temperature < 67, THEN turn_on_heater

metadata.description: Machine learning is the subset of AI focused on algorithms that analyze and “learn” the patterns of training data in order to make accurate inferences about new data.
metadata.title: What is Machine Learning? | IBM

children.page_content:
and 
IF room_temperature > 72, THEN turn_on_air_conditioner

metadata.description: Machine learning is the subset of AI focused on algorithms that analyze and “learn” the patterns of training data in order to make accurate inferences about new data.
metadata.title: What is Machine Learning? | IBM

children.page_content: the thermostat is capable of autonomous decision-making without further human intervention. At a more complex level, a large and intricate rules-based decision tree programmed by medical experts could parse symptoms, circumstances and comorbidities to aid diagnosis or prognosis.2

metadata.description: Machine learning is the subset of AI focused on algorithms that analyze and “learn” the patterns of training data in order to make accurate inferences about new data.
metadata.title: What is Machine Learning? | IBM

children.page_content: Unlike in expert systems, the logic by which a machine learning model operates isn’t explicitly programmed—it’s learned through experience. Consider a program that filters email spam: rules-based AI requires a data scientist to manually devise accurate, universal criteria for spam; machine learning requires only the selection of an appropriate algorithm and an adequate dataset of sample emails. In training, the model is shown sample emails and predicts which are spam; the error of its

metadata.description: Machine learning is the subset of AI focused on algorithms that analyze and “learn” the patterns of training data in order to make accurate inferences about new data.
metadata.title: What is Machine Learning? | IBM

children.page_content: and predicts which are spam; the error of its predictions is calculated, and its algorithm is adjusted to reduce error; this process is repeated until the model is accurate. The newly trained ML model has implicitly learned how to identify spam.

metadata.description: Machine learning is the subset of AI focused on algorithms that analyze and “learn” the patterns of training data in order to make accurate inferences about new data.
metadata.title: What is Machine Learning? | IBM

children.page_content: As the tasks an AI system is to perform become more complex, rules-based models become increasingly brittle: it’s often impossible to explicitly define every pattern and variable a model must consider. Machine learning systems have emerged as the dominant mode of artificial intelligence because implicit learning patterns from the data itself is inherently more flexible, scalable and accessible.

metadata.title: What is Machine Learning? | IBM
